newsitem.title: USA: U.S. August homebuilding strongest in 2-1/2 years.
newsitem.headline: U.S. August homebuilding strongest in 2-1/2 years.

text.p: Builders broke ground on new homes and apartments at the fastest rate in nearly 2-1/2 years during August, the Commerce Department said Thursday, as the housing industry posted a surprising surge in activity.

Construction starts, which were forecast to decline modestly, instead increased 4.5 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.525 million units -- the highest rate since 1.531 million in March 1994.

June and July building rates also were revised upward as a hearty pace of construction rolled into the third quarter and reignited fears that Federal Reserve policy makers might decide the economy was at risk of overheating.

"The continued high level of homebuilding is another strong piece of evidence that the economy still has plenty of momentum, adding pressure for the Fed to nudge short-term rates a little higher," said economist David Orr of First Union Corp. in Charlotte, N.C.

Strong job growth and rising incomes have fired up consumer confidence despite stiffer long-term interest rates that raised the 30-year mortgage rate to an average 7.95 percent in August from 7.03 percent last January.

A separate report Thursday from the Labour Department confirmed buoyant conditions in labour markets as new initial claims for unemployment claims fell 2,000 to 329,000 in the week that ended last Friday. The four-week moving average, which smoothes out seasonal variations, was up a slight 750 to 326,750.

The strong economic reports drove prices down in the bond market as concern mounted that the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee could raise short-term interest rates at its meeting on Tuesday in a bid to slow the economy's rate of expansion to curb inflation pressures.
The price of the inflation-sensitive 30-year bond dropped more than half a point and the yield, which moves in the opposite direction, rose to 7.06 percent from Wednesday's close of 7.01 percent.
On the New York Stock Exchange, the Dow Jones industrial index was down more than 6 points in early afternoon.

David Berson, an economist with the Federal National Mortgage Association, or Fannie Mae, said the housing industry "remains extremely healthy and at this point in time there are no clear signs of a downturn."

The department pushed up its estimate of July housing starts to an annual rate of 1.46 million from a previously reported 1.455 million and said June construction was at a stronger rate of 1.49 million a year, instead of 1.474 million.
Housing starts in August were nearly 9 percent above the rate a year earlier in August 1995 when building was at a rate of 1.401 million homes a year.

Particularly noteworthy was the pickup in starts on single-family homes, which generally are seen as a measure of optimism that consumers are willing and able to take on long-term financing commitments.

Construction starts on new single-family homes jumped 8.3 percent last month to a rate of 1.238 million a year after a 5.5 percent decline in July. The August starts rate on single-family homes also was the highest since March 1994, when it was at 1.28 million.
By contrast, the building rate for apartments dropped 9.5 percent to a rate of 287,000 following a 12.8 percent increase in July.
The strength in construction was broadly based. Only the Midwest posted a 2 percent decline in August to 342,000 a year but that followed a big 16 percent jump in July.

Starts in the West surged 13.5 percent to 378,000 a year and in the Northeast they gained 7 percent to a rate of 138,000. Construction in the South, the nation's biggest housing market, picked up 2.8 percent to a rate of 667,000.
